title: Internet Protocol

definition.text: The Internet Protocol (IP) is the network-layer protocol that relays datagrams across network boundaries.

facts.text: IP delivers packets from the source host to the destination host based solely on the IP addresses in the packet headers.
IP defines packet structures that encapsulate the data to be delivered and addressing methods that label each datagram with source and destination information.
Each datagram has a header, which holds the source and destination IP addresses and other metadata needed to route it, and a payload, which is the data being transported.
Nesting a data payload inside a packet with a header is called encapsulation.
The address space is divided into subnets by designating network prefixes, and addresses are assigned to host interfaces.
All hosts and routers perform IP routing; a router's main function is to carry packets across network boundaries, and routers exchange routes with each other through routing protocols.
IP's routing function enables internetworking and essentially establishes the Internet.
IPv4, the first major version, is the dominant protocol of the Internet; its successor IPv6 has been in increasing deployment on the public Internet since around 2006.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Best-effort delivery

definition.text: IP provides only best-effort delivery: it is connectionless and unreliable, and the end hosts and upper-layer protocols must repair any faults.

facts.text: The Internet follows the end-to-end principle: the network is treated as unreliable at any single element or link, so the intelligence sits in the end nodes rather than in the network.
Faults such as data corruption, packet loss and duplication may occur, and the participating end nodes must detect and compensate for all of them.
Routing is dynamic and every packet is treated independently, so packets to the same destination may take different paths and arrive out of order.
Upper-layer protocols resolve reliability issues; for example, a host may buffer network data so it reaches the application in the correct order.

IPv4 provides safeguards that the packet header is error-free: a routing node discards packets that fail the header checksum test and is not required to tell either end node about errors. IPv6 has no header checksum.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: IP addressing methods

definition.text: IP has four principal addressing methods, unicast, broadcast, multicast and anycast, which differ in how many receivers a message reaches.

facts.text: Unicast delivers a message to one specific node in a one-to-one association, because each destination address uniquely identifies a single receiver endpoint.
Broadcast delivers a message to all nodes in the network: one datagram from one sender is routed to every endpoint tied to the broadcast address, generally across an entire subnet.
Multicast delivers a message to a group of nodes that have expressed interest, with the datagram routed in a single transmission to many recipients.
Multicast differs from broadcast in that the destination address designates a subset, not necessarily all, of the accessible nodes.
Anycast delivers a message to any one node out of a group that share the same destination address, typically the nearest; the routing algorithm picks it by some distance or cost measure.
Unicast carries traffic such as HTTP, FTP and SMTP, while broadcast is used by protocols such as ARP, DHCP and NTP; a broadcast does not mean every receiver gets the message.
Multicast is used in IPTV and video conference applications, and anycast in DNS querying and CDNs.

Sending the same data to several unicast addresses means sending it once per recipient, whereas for multicast the sender sends a single datagram to the group address and the routers copy it to all interested receivers.

conflicts.text: Anycast: sender to a single device or a specific group of devices, and all other hosts in the group are also expected to receive the message.
conflicts.note: The ByteByteGo guide's party analogy has every host in the group receive the message; the encyclopedia definition has the routing algorithm pick one nearest group member.

notes: ByteByteGo calls multicast a specialized case of broadcast (b155043e03de) while the encyclopedia says multicast differs from broadcast in addressing only a subset; the encyclopedia wording is used.

title: MTU and IP fragmentation

definition.text: The maximum transmission unit (MTU) is the largest packet a link can carry, and IPv4 fragments any datagram that exceeds it.

facts.text: The size of data packets a link can carry is a technical constraint; the MTU of the local link can be examined, and Path MTU Discovery can be used for the entire path to the destination.

IPv4 automatically fragments a datagram into smaller units when the link MTU is exceeded and reorders fragments that arrive out of order; IPv6 does not fragment in network elements and requires end hosts to avoid exceeding the path MTU.
TCP adjusts its segment size to stay smaller than the MTU, while UDP and ICMP disregard MTU size and so force IP to fragment oversized datagrams.
The TCP maximum segment size should be small enough to avoid IP fragmentation, which can lead to packet loss and excessive retransmissions.
Across Ethernet the MTU is 1500 bytes and the minimum TCP and IPv4 headers are 20 bytes each, so the maximum segment size is 1500-(20+20) bytes, or 1460 bytes.
A network may split a message that is too large for the link between two nodes into fragments, send them independently and reassemble them at another node.

A larger MTU is more efficient, since each packet carries more data for the same header overhead and fewer packets need processing, but large packets hold a link longer, add delay and cost more to retransmit after an error.

Fragmentation loses the whole packet if any fragment is dropped, and it adds overhead: a tunnel header that pushes packets just over the MTU forces two fragments per packet, so every router forwards twice as many packets.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Transmission Control Protocol

definition.text: TCP is one of the main Internet protocols, providing reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications on hosts communicating over an IP network.

facts.text: TCP is connection-oriented: sender and receiver first establish a connection on agreed parameters through a three-way handshake.
TCP is a reliable byte stream service that guarantees all bytes received are identical to those sent and in the same order.
Lower layers may lose, duplicate or reorder IP packets; TCP detects this, requests retransmission of lost data, rearranges out-of-order data and helps reduce network congestion.
TCP hides networking details from the application behind a socket interface, splitting the data into segments that are encapsulated into IP datagrams and reassembled at the receiver.
Handshaking, retransmission and error detection add reliability but lengthen latency.
TCP is optimized for accurate rather than timely delivery, with delays on the order of seconds, so it is not particularly suitable for real-time applications such as voice over IP.
The Web, email, remote administration, file transfer and streaming media rely on TCP, and SSL/TLS often runs on top of it.
Applications that do not need a reliable data stream may use UDP instead, a connectionless datagram service that prioritizes time over reliability.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP connection setup and teardown
article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Connection establishment

definition.text: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake and closes it with a four-way handshake in which each side stops its own half independently.

facts.text: Before a client connects, the server must bind to and listen at a port, called a passive open; the client then performs an active open using the three-way handshake.
The client sends a SYN with a random sequence number x; the server replies with a SYN-ACK that acknowledges x + 1 and carries its own random sequence number y.
The client then sends an ACK with sequence number x + 1 and acknowledgment number y + 1; both sides have now received acknowledgments and full-duplex communication is established.
The handshake adds one round trip of latency before data can be sent, which matters a lot for short flows.
Teardown takes a four-way handshake: an endpoint that wants to stop its half sends a FIN, the other end acknowledges with an ACK, and a typical tear-down needs a FIN and ACK from each side.
After the final ACK, the side that sent the first FIN waits for a timeout (commonly 30 seconds, 1 minute or 2 minutes) with the port unavailable, so it can resend the final ACK if it was lost.
A host that closes a connection while unread incoming data remains sends an RST instead of FIN, losing the received data, so the application knows data was lost.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP reliable delivery
article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Data transfer > Reliable transmission

definition.text: TCP numbers every byte, and the receiver acknowledges what it has received so the sender can detect lost data and retransmit it.

facts.text: A sequence number identifies each byte, so the data can be rebuilt in order however it arrives; the sender picks the first sequence number on the SYN packet.
Sequence numbers let receivers discard duplicate packets and put out-of-order packets in sequence; acknowledgments let senders know when to retransmit lost packets.
An ACK tells the sender that data has been received up to a specified byte; it does not mean the data reached the application, only that delivering it is now the receiver's responsibility.
TCP uses positive acknowledgment with retransmission: the sender keeps a timer for each packet it sends and retransmits if the timer expires before an acknowledgment arrives.
TCP has two primary ways to identify loss: the retransmission timeout (RTO) and duplicate cumulative acknowledgments.
Because ACKs are cumulative, a lost segment makes the receiver repeat the acknowledgment for the last in-order packet, and this duplicate acknowledgement signals loss.
After three duplicate acknowledgments the sender retransmits the last unacknowledged packet; the threshold is three because the network may reorder segments.
On a timeout the sender retransmits the segment and doubles the timeout, which gives exponential backoff.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Selective acknowledgment
article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Selective acknowledgments

definition.text: Selective acknowledgment (SACK) is a TCP option that lets the receiver acknowledge discontinuous blocks of correctly received data, so the sender resends only what is missing.

facts.text: With only cumulative acknowledgments, if the second of ten equal segments (sequence numbers 2,000 to 2,999) is lost, the receiver can only acknowledge 2,000 and the sender may have to resend everything from 2,000.
With SACK the receiver sends a cumulative ACK of 2,000 plus a SACK option with sequence numbers 3,000 and 11,000, so the sender retransmits only the second segment.
SACK is optional, works only if both parties support it, is negotiated when the connection is established, and all popular TCP stacks support it.
SACK helps throughput by more often avoiding slow start after a loss, but TCP can selectively acknowledge a maximum of three blocks of sequence numbers.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP flow control
article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Data transfer > Flow control

definition.text: Flow control keeps a TCP sender from sending data faster than the receiver can receive and process it reliably.

facts.text: Flow control is essential where machines of diverse network speeds communicate, such as a PC sending to a smartphone that processes data slowly.

TCP uses a sliding window: each segment's receive window field states how many more bytes the receiver will buffer, and the sender may send only that much before it must wait for an acknowledgment and window update.

When the receiver advertises a window of 0 the sender stops and starts a persist timer, which protects against deadlock if the window update is lost; on expiry the sender sends a small packet to get a fresh window size.
A receiver that processes data in small increments may keep advertising a small window; this silly window syndrome is inefficient given the large TCP header overhead.
The 16-bit window size field is limited to 65,535 bytes; the window scale option raises the maximum window to 1 gigabyte for high-bandwidth networks.
The window scale option is sent only in the SYN segments during the handshake, by both sides, and its value ranges from 0 (no shift) to 14 for each direction.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP congestion control

definition.text: TCP congestion control is the set of sender-side mechanisms (a congestion window, slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery) that keep a connection from sending more than the network can carry.

facts.text: TCP uses several cooperating mechanisms to reach high performance while avoiding congestive collapse, and per the end-to-end principle congestion control is largely done by the hosts rather than the network.
Senders infer network conditions from acknowledgments, or their absence, together with timers; the retransmission timeout is based on the estimated round-trip time and its variance.

The sender keeps a congestion window (CWND) limiting unacknowledged data in flight, to protect the network; it differs from the receive window, which protects the receiver, and the sender stays within both.
Additive increase/multiplicative decrease (AIMD) grows the window linearly and cuts it multiplicatively when congestion occurs; competing AIMD flows converge toward equal shares of a contended link.
Slow start begins with a window of 1, 2, 4 or 10 MSS and adds 1 MSS per ACK, doubling the window each round trip, until a loss, the receiver's window or the slow start threshold (ssthresh) stops it.
At ssthresh TCP switches to congestion avoidance and grows the window by up to 1 MSS per round trip; after a timeout loss it saves half the window as ssthresh and restarts slow start.

Fast retransmit resends a segment after three duplicate acknowledgments instead of waiting for the timer; fast recovery then halves the window into ssthresh, skipping slow start and going straight to congestion avoidance.

Treating loss as congestion misfires on wireless links, where fading and interference cause losses and leave the radio link underused, and slow start suits short-lived connections badly, so browsers reuse or open several connections.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Port numbers

definition.text: A port number identifies a service on a host, which lets many connections share one IP address.

facts.text: A TCP connection is identified by a four-tuple of source address, source port, destination address and destination port.
TCP uses 16-bit port numbers, giving 65,536 possible values for each of the source and destination ports.
Well-known ports, assigned by IANA and used by system-level processes, include FTP (20 and 21), SSH (22), Telnet (23), SMTP (25), HTTP (80) and HTTP over SSL/TLS (443).
Registered ports run from 1024 to 49151; dynamic or private ports (49152-65535) are commonly used as ephemeral ports for temporary client connections.
NAT typically uses dynamic port numbers on its public side to tell apart traffic for many private hosts that share a single public address.
Because connection identity depends on addresses, a TCP connection is bound to one network path and breaks if an endpoint's address changes.
A UDP application binds a socket to its endpoint, an IP address plus a port, and this gives UDP application multiplexing.
Port numbers 0 through 1023 serve common well-known services, port 0 is reserved, and on Unix-like systems using a well-known port requires superuser permission.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Head-of-line blocking

definition.text: Head-of-line blocking is the delay that occurs when data that arrived later cannot be used until earlier lost or reordered data has been retransmitted and received.

facts.text: TCP offers a reliable byte stream, so the application cannot access packets that come after a lost packet until the retransmitted copy arrives.
If independent messages are multiplexed onto one TCP connection, a fully received later message must wait for the delivery of an earlier one.
Web browsers mitigate it by opening multiple parallel connections, which repeats the connection establishment cost and multiplies the resources needed to track connections.
Parallel connections run congestion control independently instead of pooling information to respond promptly to network conditions.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: SYN flood and other TCP attacks

definition.text: TCP can be attacked in several ways, including denial of service by SYN flood and connection hijacking.

facts.text: In a SYN flood, an attacker uses a spoofed IP address and repeatedly sends crafted SYN packets, so the server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections.
Proposed defenses are SYN cookies and cryptographic puzzles, though SYN cookies come with their own vulnerabilities.
An attacker who can eavesdrop on a session and redirect packets can hijack it by learning the sequence number and forging a segment that looks like the next one in the stream.
The initial sequence number should be unpredictable to defend against TCP sequence prediction attacks.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Nagle's algorithm
article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Forcing data delivery

definition.text: Nagle's algorithm makes TCP wait for a full packet of data before sending, grouping small messages into a single packet.

facts.text: TCP normally waits 200 ms for a full packet to send, which creates small but potentially serious delays when repeated constantly during a file transfer.
In Telnet each keystroke is echoed back by the server before the user sees it, so the wait would be very annoying.
Setting the TCP_NODELAY socket option overrides the default 200 ms send delay, and applications use it to force output after writing a character or a line.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: User Datagram Protocol

definition.text: UDP is a core Internet protocol that sends messages, carried as datagrams in packets, to other hosts on an IP network.

facts.text: UDP is connectionless: messages are sent without a handshake or shared connection, and a host is not expected to keep track of what it has sent.
UDP provides checksums for data integrity and port numbers for addressing different functions at the source and destination of the datagram.
UDP does not guarantee delivery, indicate the original ordering or detect duplication, and gives the sender no feedback, so the program is exposed to the unreliability of the underlying network.
If transmission reliability is wanted, the application must implement it, for example by adding its own handshaking such as confirmation that a message was received.
A UDP datagram is a header of four 2-byte fields (source port, destination port, length, checksum) followed by the payload; the checksum is optional in IPv4 and mandatory in most cases in IPv6.
The 16-bit length field sets a theoretical limit of 65,535 bytes for a datagram; the actual limit for data over IPv4 is 65,507 bytes.
Being connectionless, UDP can broadcast to all devices on the subnet, and it supports multicast, where one datagram is routed without duplication to a group of subscribers.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP versus UDP
article: User Datagram Protocol#Comparison of UDP and TCP

definition.text: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable, ordered protocol, while UDP is a simpler, connectionless, message-based protocol with no delivery guarantees.

facts.text: TCP is connection-oriented: it needs a handshake to set up end-to-end communication, after which user data may flow in both directions.
TCP is reliable: it manages acknowledgment, retransmission and timeouts and resends lost data, so there is either no missing data or, after multiple timeouts, the connection is dropped.
TCP is ordered: it buffers out-of-order data until it can be reordered and delivered. It is a byte stream with no signals marking message boundaries.
TCP is heavyweight: three packets are needed to set up a socket connection before any user data is sent, and TCP handles reliability and congestion control.
UDP is connectionless: it sends information in one direction from source to destination without verifying the readiness or state of the receiver.
UDP is unreliable and unordered: a sender cannot know whether a message arrives, there is no acknowledgment, retransmission or timeout, and arrival order is not guaranteed.
UDP is lightweight, sending packets individually with definite message boundaries, so one read at the receiver yields an entire message as it was sent.
UDP does not avoid congestion itself; congestion control must be implemented at the application level or in the network.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: UDP use cases

definition.text: UDP suits applications that value low latency over perfect delivery, such as voice, video, games and simple query-response lookups.

facts.text: Time-sensitive applications often use UDP because dropping packets is preferable to waiting for packets delayed by retransmission, and real-time communication benefits from UDP's reduced latency compared with TCP.
Streaming media, real-time multiplayer games and VoIP are typical UDP applications; loss of packets is not usually fatal, and in VoIP latency and jitter are the primary concerns.
Real-time video and audio protocols are designed to handle the occasional lost packet, so quality degrades slightly instead of suffering the large delays that retransmission would cause.
DNS queries typically use UDP for its fast, lightweight nature, though DNS can also use TCP for large responses or zone transfers; UDP suits simple query-response protocols such as DNS or NTP.

Because UDP is stateless, it suits very large numbers of clients, as in IPTV streaming; low-latency trading uses it to deliver market data to many recipients at once, and IoT devices use it to send small packets.
QUIC is a reliable and secure transport built on UDP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC and so needs a single handshake instead of separate TCP and TLS handshakes, which shortens connection setup.

title: IPv4 versus IPv6

definition.text: IPv6 replaces IPv4's 32-bit addresses with 128-bit addresses, driven by the need for more internet addresses and simpler network management.

facts.text: IPv4 uses a 32-bit address written as four dotted decimal numbers, such as 192.168.0.12, which allows approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses.
IPv6 uses a 128-bit address written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, so the internet can keep growing.
The rapid exhaustion of IPv4 address space led the IETF to redesign the Internet Protocol, which became IPv6.

The IPv4 header is more complex, with fields such as header length, time to live, header checksum and options; the IPv6 header is a simpler fixed 40 bytes with rare fields in optional extension headers, which speeds packet processing.
The two versions are in simultaneous use today, and each defines the address format differently.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time on the same devices, using whichever fits the destination address; the guide calls it one of the best approaches for a smooth transition.
IPv6's 128-bit addresses give up to approximately 3.403×10^38 addresses, which is deemed sufficient for the foreseeable future.
The IPv6 design also allows more efficient aggregation of subnetwork routing prefixes, which slows the growth of routing tables in routers.

title: Encapsulation and de-encapsulation

definition.text: Encapsulation is the nesting of a data payload inside a packet with a header, which each layer of the network stack does in turn as data is sent.

facts.text: When a device sends data over HTTP, the application layer first adds an HTTP header.
At the transport layer a TCP or UDP header is added, making a TCP segment whose header holds the source port, destination port and sequence number.
At the network layer the segment is encapsulated with an IP header that holds the source and destination IP addresses.
At the data link layer the IP datagram gets a MAC header with source and destination MAC addresses, and the frames are then sent over the physical layer as binary bits.
In precise terms, a segment is the TCP protocol data unit, a datagram is the IP unit and a frame is the data link layer unit.
The receiving device de-encapsulates by reversing the process, removing the headers layer by layer until it can read the data.
The model is layered so that each layer focuses on its own responsibilities, relying on the headers for processing instructions without needing to know the meaning of the data from the last layer.
In the OSI description each protocol data unit (PDU) contains a payload, called the service data unit (SDU), along with protocol-related headers or footers.

title: Application-layer protocols

definition.text: Network protocols are standard methods of transferring data between two computers in a network.

facts.text: HTTP is a client-server protocol for fetching resources such as HTML documents and is the foundation of data exchange on the Web; HTTPS extends it with encryption.
WebSocket gives full-duplex communication over TCP so that servers can push real-time updates, unlike REST, which always pulls; online games, stock trading and messaging apps use it.
SMTP transfers email from one user to another, and FTP transfers files between client and server using separate connections for the control channel and the data channel.
Many application-layer protocols build on TCP, while HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which relies on UDP instead of TCP for faster page responsiveness.

notes: HTTP, HTTPS and WebSocket have their own chapters; this entry only maps the protocols onto TCP or UDP.

title: IP address

definition.text: An IP address is a numerical label assigned to a device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol, so that the device can be found and addressed.

facts.text: IP addresses serve two main functions: network interface identification and location addressing.
The internet needs a way to tell computers, routers and websites apart, and IP addresses let information be sent between devices on a network.
The IP address space is managed globally by IANA and the five regional Internet registries, which hand blocks on to local registries such as ISPs and large institutions.
An IPv4 address is 32 bits, which limits the address space to 4294967296 addresses, and some are reserved for special purposes such as private networks and multicast.
IPv4 addresses are usually written in dot-decimal notation: four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, each an 8-bit octet, separated by dots, for example 192.0.2.1.
A host may deduce the geographic position of a peer by looking up the peer's IP address in a geolocation database.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Public and private IP addresses

definition.text: A public IP address is globally routable and used between hosts on the Internet, while a private address is reserved for use inside a private network.

facts.text: A public IP address is a globally routable unicast address that may be used for communication between hosts on the global Internet.
At home the public address is the one the ISP assigns to the whole network, so every connected device shares it from the outside.
Private address ranges are reserved, are not routed on the Internet and need no coordination with an address registry; a home router hands them to devices such as computers, tablets and phones.
Private networks typically reach the Internet through network address translation (NAT), which lets them conserve public address space.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Static and dynamic IP addresses

definition.text: A static IP address is configured persistently and does not change, while a dynamic IP address is assigned by the network each time a host joins or restarts.

facts.text: A static address is set by configuration and not changed, so network infrastructure such as routers and mail servers typically uses static addressing.
Static addresses are usually more expensive but more reliable, and are used for reliable geo-location services, remote access and server hosting.
Dynamic addresses are assigned by the network, most often with DHCP, which spares administrators from assigning a specific static address to each device.
Dynamic assignment lets devices share a limited address space if only some are online at a time; a DHCP address carries a lease, and an unrenewed lease may be given to another device.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: OSI model

definition.text: The OSI model is a logical, conceptual model that splits network communication into seven abstract layers, each stacked on the last.

facts.text: The OSI model describes packet transfer using layers of protocols and can be seen as a universal language for computer networking.
It has defined the common terminology used in networking discussions and documentation, which lets people take a very complex communications process apart and evaluate its components.

The model is not directly implemented in today's TCP/IP networks, but it still helps by making troubleshooting easier and by encouraging hardware makers to build products that can communicate with each other.
Thinking in layers separates a complex function into simpler components and supports a security-first mindset.
The model covers communication from transmitting bits across a physical medium up to the highest-level representation of data of a distributed application.
Each layer has well-defined functions, serves the layer above it and is served by the layer below it.
Protocols let an entity in one host interact with the corresponding entity at the same layer in another host.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: OSI model layers

definition.text: The OSI model has seven layers; from top to bottom they are application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link and physical.

facts.text: The application layer is the only one that interacts directly with user data; it provides protocols such as HTTP and SMTP that browsers and email clients rely on, though the client software is not part of it.
The presentation layer, also called the translation layer, handles translation, encryption and decryption, and compression of the application's data.

The session layer opens and closes communication between two devices, keeps the session open long enough to transfer all the data, then closes it promptly to avoid wasting resources, and synchronizes the transfer with checkpoints.
The transport layer (layer 4) is responsible for end-to-end communication between two devices: it breaks data into segments and reassembles them on the receiving device.
The network layer moves data between two different networks, breaking segments into packets and finding the best physical path to the destination, which is called routing.
The data link layer moves data between two devices on the same network, breaking packets from the network layer into smaller pieces called frames.
The physical layer covers the equipment such as cables and switches and converts data into a bit stream of 1s and 0s, with both devices agreeing on a signal convention.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Choosing between TCP and UDP

definition.text: Use TCP when data must arrive complete and in order, and use UDP when the lowest latency matters more than losing some data.

facts.text: TCP has built-in error checking and guarantees data is delivered in the order it was sent, which makes it suited to still images, data files and web pages.
TCP's feedback mechanisms make it reliable but add overhead, using more of the available network bandwidth.
UDP has no overhead for opening, maintaining or terminating a connection, and data is sent continuously whether or not the recipient receives it.
UDP is faster, simpler and more efficient than TCP, but retransmission of lost packets is only possible with TCP.
Use UDP over TCP when you need the lowest latency and late data is worse than the loss of data; it is largely preferred for real-time communication such as broadcast or multicast transmission.
Typical TCP uses are HTTPS, HTTP, SMTP, POP and FTP, while typical UDP uses are video streaming, DNS and VoIP.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Subnets and CIDR notation

definition.text: A subnet is a part of an IP network; an address is split into a network prefix and a host part, and CIDR notation states where the split falls.

facts.text: IP networks may be divided into subnetworks in both IPv4 and IPv6, by designating network prefixes within the address space.
An IP address has two parts: the network prefix in the high-order bits and the remaining bits, called the host identifier (the interface identifier in IPv6), used for host numbering within a network.
The subnet mask or CIDR notation determines how the address divides into network and host parts; the term subnet mask is used only within IPv4, but both versions use CIDR.

In CIDR notation the address is followed by a slash and the number of bits of the network part; 192.0.2.1 with mask 255.255.255.0 is written 192.0.2.1/24 because the first 24 bits indicate the network.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Network address translation

definition.text: Network address translation (NAT) maps one IP address space into another by rewriting address information in packet headers as they cross a routing device, so a whole private network can share one public address.

facts.text: NAT conserves IPv4 address space: 32-bit IPv4 addresses can identify about 4.3 billion devices, and one Internet-routable address on a NAT gateway can serve an entire private network.

Basic NAT is a one-to-one translation that changes only IP addresses and the checksums that include them; the common one-to-many form maps many private hosts to one public address and is what people usually mean by NAT.

A router with a private and a public interface typically does the NAT: it rewrites outbound source addresses to its public address, usually assigned by the ISP, and tracks each active connection so replies reach the right host.

For TCP and UDP the port numbers are rewritten too (network address and port translation, also called PAT or IP masquerading), so the address and port pair on a returning packet maps back to one private host.
The NAT device keeps a translation table of internal address, original source port and translated port; an incoming packet whose destination port is not in the table is dropped or rejected.

Because the first outbound packet creates the mapping, conversations can only start from the private side, and outside hosts cannot initiate a connection to an internal host unless destination NAT (port forwarding) publishes the service.

NAT breaks end-to-end connectivity: protocols that embed addresses in their data (FTP, SIP), VoIP and other peer-to-peer applications need application-level gateways or NAT traversal, and NAT complicates IPsec integrity checks.
NAT is not commonly used in IPv6, because the large address space lets every device have a unique globally routable address and restores end-to-end connectivity.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP/IP model

definition.text: The TCP/IP model, also called the Internet protocol suite, organizes the Internet's protocols into four layers (link, internet, transport and application) according to each protocol's scope.

facts.text: The suite provides end-to-end data communication, specifying how data is packetized, addressed, transmitted, routed and received; its foundational protocols are TCP, UDP and IP.
The link layer covers the local network link, which includes all hosts reachable without crossing a router; TCP/IP is hardware independent and can run over virtual links such as VPNs and tunnels.

The internet layer routes data between independent networks using hierarchical IP addressing; it offers an unreliable datagram service that forwards each datagram to a next-hop router and does not distinguish between transport protocols.

The transport layer gives applications host-to-host data channels, connection-oriented through TCP or connectionless through UDP, and uses port numbers for process-specific channels; it may add error control, segmentation, flow control and congestion control.

The application layer holds protocols such as HTTP, FTP, SMTP and DHCP; their data is encapsulated into TCP streams or UDP datagrams, and formatting and presentation are left to libraries and APIs rather than extra layers.
An application sends its data down through the layers, and the data is encapsulated further at each level.

The original end-to-end principle kept state and intelligence at the edges and a simple network between them; real-world firewalls, network address translators and web caches have since forced changes.

TCP/IP's application layer covers the OSI application, presentation and most of the session layers, its transport layer maps to OSI transport, the internet layer to part of the network layer, and the link layer to the data link layer.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Transport layer
article: OSI model#Layer architecture > Layer 4: Transport layer

definition.text: The transport layer carries variable-length data sequences from an application on a source host to an application on a destination host across a network.

facts.text: Transport protocols may be connection-oriented or connectionless.

Segmentation breaks large data units or long streams into segments because the network layer imposes an MTU; a segment must be small enough to leave room for the network-layer and transport-layer headers.
Segmentation is an optional function: connection-oriented protocols such as TCP segment and reassemble data, while connectionless protocols such as UDP usually do not.
The transport layer can control reliability through flow control, error control and acknowledgments; stateful, connection-oriented protocols track segments and retransmit those that fail delivery.
Reliability is not a strict requirement of the transport layer: protocols such as UDP serve applications willing to accept some packet loss, reordering, errors or duplication.

TCP and UDP were not developed under the OSI model but are commonly categorized as layer 4 protocols, while TLS does not strictly fit the model and combines transport and presentation layer characteristics.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Network layer
article: OSI model#Layer architecture > Layer 3: Network layer

definition.text: The network layer transfers packets from one node to another across different networks, finding a route through intermediate nodes where needed.

facts.text: In a network every node has an address, and a sender only supplies the message content and the destination address while the network finds the way, possibly routing through intermediate nodes.
If a message is too large for the data link layer between two nodes, the network may split it into fragments, send them independently and reassemble them at another node.
Network-layer delivery is not necessarily reliable: a protocol may, but need not, report delivery errors or provide reliable delivery.
If the two communicating devices are on the same network, the network layer is unnecessary.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: NAT traversal
article: Network address translation#Type of NAT and NAT traversal, role of port preservation for TCP

definition.text: NAT traversal is the set of techniques, such as port forwarding and TCP hole punching, that let peers behind different NATs communicate with each other.

facts.text: NAT traversal problems arise when peers behind different NATs try to communicate; port forwarding or traversal techniques solve them, and VoIP, videoconferencing and other peer-to-peer applications must use them to work.

A client may need to find its external address and the type of mapping its NAT uses; STUN was specified for this, and its original split into full-cone, restricted-cone, port-restricted and symmetric NAT has been deprecated.
RFC 4787 separates NAT mapping from NAT filtering: security is determined by the filtering behavior, and a NAT MUST have endpoint-independent mapping.

TCP hole punching, the most popular TCP traversal technique, needs the NAT to preserve ports for outgoing TCP connections; UDP needs no port preservation because many UDP communications can share one source port.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

definition.text: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices on a network, using a client-server architecture.

facts.text: A central DHCP server manages a pool of addresses and parameters such as default gateway, domain name, name servers and time servers, so devices need no manual configuration; many routers and residential gateways include a DHCP server.
DHCP is connectionless and runs over UDP: the server listens on port 67 and the client on port 68, and a client joining the network sends a broadcast query for its configuration.

A server allocates addresses three ways: dynamic (a leased address from a reserved range, reclaimed if unrenewed), automatic (a permanent address from a range) and manual (an administrator maps a client ID or MAC address to an IP address).
A client's broadcast stays on its own subnet, so relay agents on routers forward it by unicast to configured DHCP servers; the GIADDR field tells the server which subnet's address pool to use.

Base DHCP has no authentication: a rogue DHCP server can hand clients false information such as a DNS server, enabling denial-of-service or man-in-the-middle attacks, and a client can exhaust the address pool with fresh identifiers.

Option 82 lets operators tag DHCP messages on their trusted network as an authorization token, while the RFC 3118 authentication extension has never been widely deployed because of key management problems.
DHCPv6 is the IPv6 version, different enough to count as a separate protocol; IPv6 hosts may instead use stateless address autoconfiguration.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: DHCP lease process

definition.text: A DHCP client obtains an IP address through four exchanges (discovery, offer, request and acknowledgement) and then holds it as a lease that it must renew.

facts.text: The client starts with a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast to 255.255.255.255 or the subnet broadcast address, and may ask for a particular address that the server can take into account.
A server that gets the discover reserves an address and replies with DHCPOFFER, which carries the offered IP address, subnet mask, lease duration and the server's own address.
The client may receive several offers but accepts only one, broadcasting a DHCPREQUEST that names the chosen server; the other servers withdraw their offers and return those addresses to their pools.
The server completes the exchange with a DHCPACK that carries the lease duration and any other configuration the client asked for, ending the IP configuration process.
Before claiming an address, the client should probe it, for example with ARP, to see whether another host already uses it; a server may likewise ping an address before reusing it.

Clients start renewing once half the lease interval has passed, unicasting DHCPREQUEST to the granting server; if it stays unreachable the client rebinds by broadcasting the request so any server can renew the lease.
When a lease expires the client must stop using the address and restart with a DHCPDISCOVER; since its address then changes, any ongoing connections break.
A client may send DHCP Release to give up its address, but the protocol does not require it because devices are often unplugged without warning.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Address Resolution Protocol

definition.text: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the link-layer address, such as a MAC address, that goes with an internet-layer address, typically an IPv4 address.

facts.text: ARP lets a host send an IPv4 packet to another node on its local network: it broadcasts a request containing the target's IP address, and the node holding that address replies with its MAC address.
ARP is a request-response protocol whose messages are carried directly in link-layer frames; it works only within one subnetwork and is never routed.
In the standard example, A broadcasts an ARP request to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF for 192.168.0.55; only B answers with its MAC address, and A then sends the data packet addressed to B's MAC.
Nodes keep a lookup cache of IP-to-MAC mappings so they need not broadcast every time, and B can cache A's mapping from the request it received.
Before using an IPv4 address, a host must broadcast ARP probes to detect a conflict; a gratuitous ARP announcement solicits no reply and updates other hosts' cached mappings when an address changes.

ARP cannot authenticate replies, so a spoofer can answer for another system's address to intercept its traffic in a man-in-the-middle or denial-of-service attack, while a proxy ARP answers on another system's behalf by design.
In IPv6 networks, the Neighbor Discovery Protocol provides the function of ARP.
RFC 826 and RFC 1122 place ARP in the link layer, but other textbooks put it in the OSI data link layer, the network layer or an intermediate layer 2.5.

contested_note: Sources place ARP in the link layer, the OSI data link layer, the network layer or an intermediate layer 2.5.
chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: QUIC

definition.text: QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol normally layered on UDP that multiplexes streams over a connection and builds TLS into its handshake, designed to replace TCP for many applications.

facts.text: TCP treats any error as blocking, so when several HTTP/2 streams share one TCP connection a single lost packet stalls all of them; this is head-of-line blocking.

QUIC uses UDP, which has no loss recovery, and does recovery itself: each stream is flow-controlled separately and lost data is retransmitted at the QUIC level, so an error in one stream does not block the others.

QUIC makes the exchange of TLS setup keys and the list of supported protocols part of the initial handshake, instead of setting up an unencrypted pipe and then negotiating security, which cuts connection setup latency.
QUIC encrypts packets individually so encrypted data never waits for partial packets; under TCP the encryption records sit in a bytestream whose higher-layer boundaries the protocol stack cannot see.

Every QUIC packet carries a connection identifier, so a connection survives an IP address change such as a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular, whereas TCP connections time out one by one and must be re-established.

QUIC can be implemented in application space rather than the operating system kernel, and moves congestion control into user space at both endpoints, so updates and new algorithms need no kernel change.

Many middleboxes rate-limit or block UDP, so Chromium starts a QUIC and a TCP connection at the same time and falls back to TCP with negligible latency; QUIC also minimises its wire image to resist ossification.
The IETF standardized QUIC in RFC 9000 in May 2021, using TLS 1.3; HTTP/3 was its first application, and DNS-over-QUIC and SMB over QUIC are others.

notes: Distinct from the HTTP chapter's 'HTTP/3 and QUIC' entry, which is about HTTP/3; this entry teaches the QUIC transport itself.
chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Path MTU Discovery
article: Maximum transmission unit#Internet protocol > Path MTU Discovery

definition.text: Path MTU Discovery is a technique for finding the smallest MTU along the route between two IP hosts, so packets can be sized to avoid fragmentation.

facts.text: The path MTU is the smallest MTU of any hop between source and destination, that is, the largest packet that crosses the path without fragmentation; Path MTU Discovery finds it and is defined for both IPv4 and IPv6.

The sender sets the DF (don't fragment) bit; a device with a smaller MTU drops the packet and returns an ICMP Datagram Too Big message giving its MTU, and the sender lowers its estimate and repeats until packets fit.

Networks that drop ICMP traffic, for example to resist denial-of-service attacks, break discovery; Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is more robust to ICMP filtering, and a changing route can change the path MTU mid-transfer.
A failed discovery lets a connection work for small data but stall once a host sends a large block; one workaround is to change the maximum segment size in the TCP setup packet at one's firewall.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP congestion control algorithms

definition.text: TCP congestion control algorithms are variants of the window-adjustment rules, such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR, that differ in how they detect and react to congestion.

facts.text: Tahoe and Reno both treat a retransmission timeout and three duplicate ACKs as loss; on duplicate ACKs Tahoe drops the window to 1 MSS and restarts slow start, while Reno halves it and enters fast recovery.
CUBIC, a less aggressive derivative of BIC, makes the window a cubic function of time since the last congestion event; it is the default in Linux since kernel 2.6.19, and on Android and macOS.

Unlike loss-based algorithms, BBR (Google, 2016) builds a network model from the maximum bandwidth and round-trip time delivered; BBRv1's fairness is disputed, as it can take the link from a coexisting CUBIC flow.

Algorithms can be grouped by network awareness: black box ones use only binary congestion feedback, grey box ones use time measurements such as RTT variation and arrival rate, and green box ones use explicit feedback from the network.

contested_note: The fairness of BBR version 1 toward other flows is disputed: Google's presentation shows it coexisting with CUBIC, while researchers found it unfair.
chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Network socket

definition.text: A network socket is a software endpoint in a network node for sending and receiving data across a network, identified externally by its protocol, IP address and port number.

facts.text: A socket exists only during the lifetime of an application process; the networking API defines its structure and gives the application a socket descriptor, which on Unix-like systems is a type of file descriptor.
In TCP and UDP a socket address is an IP address plus a port number, like a phone number plus an extension; Internet sockets use it to deliver incoming packets to the right application process.

The operating system's protocol stack extracts the socket address from the IP and transport headers and hands the payload to the matching application; Internet socket APIs are usually based on the Berkeley sockets standard.
Stream sockets, usually TCP, give a reliable, ordered flow of data; datagram sockets, using UDP, address and route each packet individually, with no guarantee of order or delivery.
Raw sockets send and receive IP packets without transport-layer formatting, while other socket types encapsulate the payload automatically.
A server creates a socket in the listening state and waits for clients; a TCP server creates a dedicated socket for each client connection, serving it in a new process or thread.
Many established TCP sockets can share one local IP address and port, because each socket pair is identified by a unique 4-tuple of source and destination addresses and ports.
UDP sockets have no established state: one UDP server socket handles datagrams from all clients, identified only by the local address, while stateful firewalls and NATs track active socket pairs.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Internet Control Message Protocol

definition.text: The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is a supporting protocol that routers and other network devices use to send error messages and operational information about IP communication.

facts.text: ICMP reports problems such as an unavailable service or an unreachable host or router; errors are directed to the source IP address of the packet that caused them.
Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP does not normally carry data between systems or serve end-user applications, apart from diagnostic tools such as ping and traceroute, and an ICMP packet has no port number.
ICMP is a network-layer protocol and an integral part of IP: its messages travel inside IPv4 packets under protocol number 1, and IPv6 uses a separate ICMPv6.

Every ICMP packet has an eight-byte header whose type and code identify the message; error messages include the offending IP header plus at least eight bytes of its data so the host can match the error to a process.
Each forwarding router decrements the IP time to live; at 0 the packet is discarded and an ICMP time exceeded message goes to the source.

Ping uses ICMP echo request and echo reply, while traceroute sends datagrams with increasing TTL values and reads the time exceeded and destination unreachable messages to find each router on the path.

Destination unreachable is sent when the host cannot be reached, the protocol or port is not active, or a packet must be fragmented but has the don't-fragment flag set, which Path MTU Discovery relies on.
ICMP Redirect lets a router tell a host that a better route to a destination goes through another router on the host's own subnet, so the host should send those packets directly there.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Client-server model

definition.text: The client-server model splits the work of a distributed application between servers, which provide a resource or service, and clients, which request it.

facts.text: Clients start communication sessions and servers wait for incoming requests; a client usually shares none of its own resources, and client and server may even run on the same device.

Servers are classified by the service they offer, such as web or file serving, and one computer can run several server programs; whether a machine is a client, a server or both depends on the application.

Clients and servers exchange messages in a request-response pattern defined by an application-layer protocol; the service abstracts the server's work, so the client only has to understand the response.
A server may expose an API as an abstraction layer for its service: restricting messages to a specific content format eases parsing, and abstracting access eases cross-platform data exchange.
In online banking the browser asks a web server, which acts as a client of a database server; an application server applies the business logic and the web server returns the result.
A server receiving many requests relies on scheduling to prioritize them and may limit clients to prevent abuse; denial-of-service attacks overload it with excessive request rates.
Work runs server-side when it needs data or functions the client lacks, or would be slow, unreliable or insecure on the client; client-side work saves time, bandwidth and security risk.

The server is often a centralized system serving many clients, sized to the expected workload and scaled beyond one machine with load balancing and failover; peer-to-peer designs instead let equal peers share load and resources directly.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP three-way handshake
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.5. Establishing a Connection

definition.text: The three-way handshake is the procedure TCP uses to establish a connection, in which the two peers exchange and acknowledge each other's initial sequence numbers.

facts.text: Each side sends a SYN carrying its own initial sequence number and needs it acknowledged; the acknowledgment of the first SYN and the second side's own SYN travel in one segment, which makes three messages.
The handshake is needed because sequence numbers are not tied to a global clock; the receiver of a first SYN cannot know whether it is an old one, so it asks the sender to verify it.
The principal reason for the three-way handshake is to prevent old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion.
In the basic exchange the first SYN uses sequence number 100, so the reply acknowledges 101; a bare ACK takes no sequence space, because otherwise acknowledgments would themselves need acknowledging.

If an old duplicate SYN reaches the passive peer, it replies normally; the first peer sees the wrong acknowledgment, sends a RST, the passive peer returns to LISTEN, and the genuine SYN then completes the handshake.
The handshake also works when both peers open at once: each receives a SYN without an acknowledgment after sending its own, and an implementation MUST support this simultaneous open.
Handshake segments may carry data, but the receiver must buffer it and not deliver it to the application until the connection reaches ESTABLISHED.

notes: RFC 9293 account of the handshake; titled to resolve the many prerequisite references to 'TCP three-way handshake'. The existing 'TCP connection setup and teardown' covers handshake and teardown from Wikipedia.
chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP sequence numbers

definition.text: TCP gives every octet of data on a connection a sequence number, which lets the receiver acknowledge, order and de-duplicate what it receives.

facts.text: Every octet is sequenced and so can be acknowledged; acknowledgments are cumulative, so an acknowledgment of X means all octets up to but not including X have arrived, which makes duplicate detection straightforward.
The sequence number space is finite, from 0 to 2^32 - 1, so all sequence number arithmetic is done modulo 2^32.
SYN and FIN are the only controls that occupy sequence space, so they can be retransmitted and acknowledged without confusion; a SYN counts as before the first data octet and a FIN as after the last.

A connection can be reused, and each new instance is an incarnation; TCP must not mistake duplicate segments from an earlier incarnation for new ones, which TIME-WAIT and initial sequence number selection together prevent.
A new connection takes a 32-bit initial sequence number from a clock that typically ticks about every 4 microseconds and cycles in roughly 4.55 hours, much longer than the Maximum Segment Lifetime.

Implementations SHOULD set the initial sequence number to a timer value plus a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key; it must not be computable from outside, or an attacker could guess sequence numbers.
Using up 2^32 octets of sequence space takes 4.5 hours at 2 megabits/sec, 5.4 minutes at 100 megabits/sec, 34 seconds at 1 Gbps, 3 seconds at 10 Gbps and around a third of a second at 100 Gbps.
At high data rates the sequence space can wrap within the segment lifetime, so TCP Timestamp Options and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) are needed to detect and discard old duplicates.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP connection states
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.3. TCP Terminology Overview > 3.3.2. State Machine Overview

definition.text: A TCP connection moves through a fixed set of states during its life, changing state in response to user calls, incoming segments and timeouts.

facts.text: The states are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and the fictional CLOSED, which means no connection record exists.
State changes are caused by the user calls OPEN, SEND, RECEIVE, CLOSE, ABORT and STATUS, by incoming segments carrying SYN, ACK, RST or FIN, and by timeouts.
A passive OPEN means the process wants to accept incoming connection requests; an active OPEN attempts to initiate a connection.
Opening: LISTEN waits for a request from any remote peer, SYN-SENT has sent a request and awaits a matching one, and SYN-RECEIVED has both received and sent one and awaits the acknowledgment.
ESTABLISHED is an open connection and the normal state for the data transfer phase, in which received data can be delivered to the user.

Closing: FIN-WAIT-1 and FIN-WAIT-2 wait for the peer's termination request, CLOSE-WAIT waits for the local user to close, and CLOSING and LAST-ACK wait for acknowledgment of a termination request already sent.
TIME-WAIT waits long enough to be sure the peer received the acknowledgment of its termination request and to keep delayed segments from earlier connections from affecting new ones.
A RST can be sent from any state and leads to TIME-WAIT, while receiving a RST from any state leads to LISTEN or CLOSED; the state diagram is only a summary, not the full specification.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TIME-WAIT state
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.6. Closing a Connection

definition.text: TIME-WAIT is the state in which the endpoint that closed a TCP connection first lingers, so that late segments from the old connection cannot disturb a new one.

facts.text: A connection closed actively MUST linger in TIME-WAIT for 2xMSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), and this specification takes the MSL to be 2 minutes.
TIME-WAIT limits the rate of connection reuse, so that segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection are not confused with the new one.

A host in TIME-WAIT MAY accept a new SYN from the remote endpoint to reopen the connection directly, and a Timestamp-based algorithm that shortens TIME-WAIT supports higher connection establishment rates on busy servers.
The side that issues a reset should also enter TIME-WAIT, since this generally helps to reduce the load on busy servers.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP reset
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.5. Establishing a Connection > 3.5.2. Reset Generation

definition.text: A reset (RST) segment tells a TCP peer that a segment does not belong to a live connection, so the receiver ignores it or aborts the connection.

facts.text: A RST is sent whenever a segment arrives that apparently is not meant for the current connection, such as a SYN that matches no existing connection, and it must not be sent if that is unclear.
A RST is valid if its sequence number is in the receive window, or in SYN-SENT if its ACK acknowledges the SYN; the receiver validates it first and only then changes state.
A receiver in LISTEN ignores a RST; in SYN-RECEIVED it returns to LISTEN if it arrived by a passive open, else aborts; in any other state it aborts the connection and tells the user.

A half-open connection exists when one peer closed, aborted or lost its state without the other knowing; it is reset automatically when either side tries to send data, as the peer with no connection answers with a reset.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP half-close
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.6. Closing a Connection > 3.6.1. Half-Closed Connections

definition.text: Because TCP closes the two directions of a connection independently, an endpoint can stop sending while it keeps receiving.

facts.text: CLOSE means 'I have no more data to send'; TCP treats it as simplex, so the closing user can keep receiving until the remote peer has closed too.
An endpoint that receives a FIN acknowledges it but does not send its own FIN until its user also closes; all data sent before the CLOSE is delivered reliably, in both directions.

A half-closed connection is closed in one direction only and the host may keep sending in the other; a host MAY instead implement a half-duplex close in which the application cannot keep reading after CLOSE.
A host using the half-duplex close SHOULD send a RST if data is still pending when CLOSE is called or arrives afterwards, to show that data was lost.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP segmentation and MSS

definition.text: Segmentation is how TCP cuts an application's byte stream into segments, and the Maximum Segment Size option tells the peer the largest segment it will accept.

facts.text: Segment boundaries need not match the application's send calls: TCP guarantees no correlation between the boundaries of segments and those of the application's read or write buffers.
Larger segments mean fewer packets in flight, fewer interrupts and layer crossings, and less header overhead, though the benefit shrinks as segments grow.

Smaller segments avoid a datagram larger than the smallest MTU on the path, which means loss or fragmentation, and avoid delaying the data stream; some firewalls and middleboxes drop fragmented packets or the ICMP messages about them.
Endpoints MUST implement sending and receiving the MSS option, and SHOULD send it in every SYN when their receive MSS differs from the default.
Without an MSS option the default send MSS is 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6.
The effective send MSS must be the smaller of the peer's advertised MSS, which reflects its reassembly buffer, and the largest size the IP layer permits, less the TCP header and any IP options.
The MSS to advertise should be the effective MTU minus the fixed IP and TCP headers; when options are present, the sender must shrink the data in each packet by the option bytes.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP retransmission timeout
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.1. Retransmission Timeout

definition.text: The retransmission timeout (RTO) is how long a TCP sender waits for an acknowledgment before resending a segment, and it must be determined dynamically.

facts.text: Segments may be lost to errors or congestion, so TCP retransmits to ensure delivery of every segment, and duplicate segments may arrive because of network or TCP retransmission.
Because networks vary so much, the RTO must be determined dynamically, computed by the RFC 6298 algorithm including Karn's algorithm for taking RTT samples.
Successive RTO values for the same segment back off exponentially, and the backed-off value is kept until a segment with new data has been sent and acknowledged without retransmission.

An endpoint MUST implement slow start, congestion avoidance and exponential backoff of RTO to avoid congestion collapse; other algorithms are allowed if they conform to the IETF Standards Track specifications.

Excessive retransmission of one segment signals a remote host or path failure: at threshold R1 TCP gives negative advice to IP to trigger dead-gateway diagnosis, and at a larger R2 it closes the connection.
R1 SHOULD correspond to at least 3 retransmissions at the current RTO and R2 to at least 100 seconds, and TCP SHOULD tell the application of the delivery problem once R1 is reached.
An application MUST be able to set R2 per connection; an interactive application might set it to infinity so the user decides when to disconnect.
Opening a connection can fail through excessive SYN retransmissions, a RST or an ICMP Port Unreachable, and R2 for a SYN MUST allow retransmission for at least 3 minutes.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: TCP keep-alive
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.4. TCP Keep-Alives

definition.text: A TCP keep-alive sends a probe on an idle connection to check that the peer is still there.

facts.text: TCP does not inherently detect whether a peer is alive; keep-alives are optional, not universally accepted, and where offered they send a probe segment designed to elicit a response from the peer.

A connection is idle when no segments have arrived for a long time and nothing new or unacknowledged is waiting to be sent; the probe usually has sequence number SND.NXT-1 and may carry one garbage octet.

Keep-alives MUST default to off with a per-connection switch, and are sent only when nothing is outstanding and nothing has arrived within a configurable interval that MUST default to no less than two hours.
Because ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted, a keep-alive MUST NOT treat the failure to answer one probe as proof that the connection is dead.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Delayed acknowledgment
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.3. Delayed Acknowledgments -- When to Send an ACK Segment

definition.text: A delayed ACK means a receiver sends fewer than one acknowledgment per data segment received, which saves effort in both the network and the hosts.

facts.text: A TCP endpoint SHOULD delay ACKs but never excessively: the delay MUST be less than 0.5 seconds.
An ACK SHOULD be generated for at least every second full-sized segment, or 2*RMSS bytes of new data, where RMSS is the MSS specified by the endpoint receiving the segments.

Excessive ACK delays disturb round-trip timing and packet clocking, so out-of-order segments, segments above a gap and segments that fill a gap should be acknowledged immediately to speed loss recovery.

Nagle's algorithm combined with delayed ACKs, both on by default in common operating systems, can badly hurt request-response applications, and many applications simply disable Nagle with a socket option.

chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

title: Silly window syndrome
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.2. Silly Window Syndrome Avoidance

definition.text: Silly window syndrome is a stable pattern of small incremental window movements that leaves TCP performing extremely poorly.

facts.text: A TCP implementation MUST include SWS avoidance in both sender and receiver; Nagle's algorithm curbs tiny segments from small data increments, while SWS avoidance curbs small segments from the window edge advancing in small steps.

The receiver avoids advancing its right window edge in small increments: it keeps the edge fixed until the freed space reaches the smaller of a fraction (recommended 1/2) of its buffer and the effective send MSS.
The sender transmits only if a maximum-sized segment fits, or pushed data can all be sent, or at least a fraction (recommended 1/2) of the largest window seen fits, or an override timeout fires.
The sender cannot see the receiver's buffer, so it estimates it as the maximum send window seen; an override timeout of 0.1 - 1.0 seconds forces data out so a wrong estimate cannot deadlock.

title: Zero-window probing
article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.1. Zero-Window Probing

definition.text: Zero-window probing is how a TCP sender keeps testing a receiver whose window is zero, so that the reopening of the window is reliably reported.

facts.text: Even when the send window is zero, the sender must regularly transmit at least one octet of new data, or retransmit, to probe the window; this guarantees that the window reopening is reported reliably.
The first probe SHOULD be sent once a zero window has lasted the retransmission timeout, and the interval between successive probes SHOULD increase exponentially.
A receiver MAY keep its window closed indefinitely, and the sender MUST keep the connection open as long as the receiver keeps acknowledging probes, as in the 'printer ran out of paper' case.
A receiver SHOULD NOT shrink the window by moving its right edge left, but a sender MUST be robust against it, and a window that shrinks to zero MUST be probed.

title: TCP segment header

definition.text: A TCP header follows the IP header and carries the fields TCP needs: ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window and checksum.

facts.text: The header holds 16-bit source and destination ports, a 32-bit sequence number (the initial sequence number when SYN is set) and a 32-bit acknowledgment number that is always sent once a connection is established.

The control bits, also called flags, are CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN; the Data Offset counts the 32-bit words in the header, so the header, even with options, is a multiple of 32 bits long.
The 16-bit window field says how many data octets, beginning at the one in the acknowledgment field, the sender of the segment will accept; the value is shifted when window scaling is used.
The checksum is never optional: the sender MUST generate it and the receiver MUST check it, and it covers a pseudo-header of IP information, which protects the connection against misrouted segments.
